chapter_theme: The chaste wife (கற்புடை மகளிர்): her worth is measured by self-guarding, hospitality in poverty, modesty that never wears off, and timely sulking. In the last four quatrains she speaks herself, as a wife wronged by a husband who goes to courtesans.
structure_note: 381-386 describe the good wife, and 385 is already in her voice. 387-390 are her complaints about her straying husband, two of them addressed to the minstrel who carries his messages (388, 390); Mudaliar says 387 shows the wife's own purity, which is why such speeches stand in this chapter.

381.reading: Even among women as famous as Indrani for a chastity hard to attain, the fragrant-browed woman who keeps the quality that leaves no man following her in desire is the good companion.
381.nuance: Pope reads it differently: the absence of admirers is a help to women who guard themselves, as though even the chaste benefit from not being tempted. Both commentators make the absence her own doing. Indrani is the standard of the comparison, so the claim is strong: even such women are measured by this.

382.reading: Even in hard times, when the household cooks with a single pot of water, and even if kin arrive enough to drink the sea dry, the soft-spoken woman who keeps her duties as her settled way is the glory of the home.
382.nuance: The two hyperboles push in opposite directions, one pot against a sea, and her duty holds between them. Shanmuganar names the duty as hospitality.

383.reading: Though the house is open on all four sides, tiny, and dripping with rain from the roof everywhere, where the excellent wife lives, capable in the highest virtues and praised by the town she lives in, that alone is a home.
383.nuance: Mudaliar draws the consequence the verse leaves unsaid, that other houses are forests, which completes the pair with 361.

384.reading: She is a wife who is lovely to the eye, adorns herself as her husband loves, holds him in awe, has the modesty that is shy before the town, and, in awe of him, knows when to sulk and relents sweetly: the soft-spoken woman.
384.nuance: Mudaliar gives two senses of ஊர்நாண் இயல்பினாள்: one who is shy before the townsfolk, or one whose conduct puts the townsfolk to shame. The translation attached to 383 in Pope's text takes the second. Sulking is counted among a good wife's virtues, provided it is well timed and quickly ended.

385.reading: However often our husband rises from our shoulders, we feel as shy as if we were seeing him for the first time; how, then, do those who embrace many men's chests for gain do it every day?
385.nuance: The wife speaks with wonder rather than scorn: she can't imagine the life she sets against her own.

386.reading: Like the learning of one with understanding in his heart, like bright wealth in the hands of a generous man, like a sharp sword in the hand of a clear-minded hero, is the beauty a modest woman has.
386.nuance: The verse gives three similes and no explanation. Mudaliar supplies one: learning and a giver's wealth serve everyone, but a hero's sword destroys whoever stands against it, so a modest woman's beauty serves her husband alone and ruins any other who desires it. Shanmuganar pairs the first two similes as both useful and calls the sword only notable.

387.reading: The lord of the town has bought, it seems, black gram and red gram, a tuni and a pathakku, all as one; the mountain-chested man who embraced bright-browed women unlike me comes, without bathing, to embrace me too.
387.nuance: The grain proverb is the wife's charge of indiscrimination: he treats the courtesans and his wife as one measure. Mudaliar says the verse shows the wife's own purity.

388.reading: Minstrel, don't speak cruel words; if you must, step softly aside and go: to the lord of the town we are like the drum's left face, so tell it to those who are like its right face.
388.nuance: The right face of the துடி is struck and the left isn't, as Mudaliar explains: the wife calls herself the side that is no longer played. The minstrel is the husband's go-between.

389.reading: I am the one who grieved if a fly so much as flew over the lord of the cool town where water gleams once the reeds are pulled; and I am the one who has sat looking at his chest, its cool sandal paste smeared by breasts that struck it till sparks flew.
389.nuance: The repeated 'I am the one' sets two times side by side without comment, and the grief lies in the gap between them.

390.reading: Minstrel, don't tell the great lie that the man with the garland of opening buds will be kind to us; to the lord of the town we are like the end joints of the sugar-cane, so tell it to those who are like the middle joints.
390.nuance: Mudaliar gives the situation: the husband, back from a courtesan and refused, sends the minstrel to soothe her, and she mocks the messenger.

links.note: On the commentators' reading, both place a wife's chastity in her own keeping: 57 calls the guard of her own steadfastness the best, and 381 praises the woman whose conduct leaves no one pursuing her. On Pope's reading, 381 instead credits the absence of temptation.
51's good wife lives within her husband's means; 382's good wife keeps her duties of hospitality even when the means are one pot of water and the guests could drink the sea.

The two halves of one claim: 361's mansion without a good wife is a wilderness, and 383's leaking hut with one is the only true home. Mudaliar's gloss on 383, that other houses are forests, makes the pairing explicit.
1302 says sulking is right in measure like salt and spoils if prolonged; 384's good wife sulks at the right moment and relents sweetly.

385's wife never loses her shyness with her husband however often they meet; 1257's woman knows nothing of shame when her beloved does what she desires. The second describes desire overriding reserve after separation, so the two set limits on each other rather than conflict.
Both wives refuse a chest that other women have shared: 1311 because all women feast on him with their eyes, and 387 because he comes from the courtesans unbathed.
The same speech to the minstrel in the same frame, with two images of the neglected side: the unstruck face of the drum and the sapless end joints of the sugar-cane.
Both wives read the courtesans' embraces on the husband's chest, unwashed in 387 and smeared with sandal in 389.

source_issues: 383: Pope's text runs on into his translation of 384 ('The wife: placens uxor ...'), and 384 has no Pope translation aligned.
385: the Tamil reads பெருள்நசையால், apparently a misprint for பொருள்நசையால்.
386: Shanmuganar's field opens with the stray heading இன்ப வியல்.
390: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of chapter 40.
